job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Freya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a bedroom with my older sister Greta, a nurse, in a flat above a laundrette in Brightmoor. She works nights, so I tiptoe in the mornings. My day is a stack of tabs: job boards, a spreadsheet tracking every application, and an AI assistant that helps me prep for each interview by quizzing me. In the afternoons I write a small weekly newsletter on money basics for students, which has about three hundred readers and earns nothing yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and what did the internships involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Business and finance with a minor in marketing, and I was top of my year. One internship was at a startup that sells subscription boxes, Pennant & Pine, where I tracked customer numbers and built their first monthly dashboard. The other was at a large insurer, in the finance planning team, mostly updating forecasts. I liked the startup better, because I could see the effect of what I built within a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and not a miracle. I already use it every day, and it saves time but doesn't do my thinking. I'd tell friends to treat it like a calculator: great when you know what you're asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my situation wouldn't change. I'd still be a graduate with no offer, some debt and about two months saved, and a sister who covers my half of the grocery shop when I'm short. The quiet-AI world is the same as today, which isn't great for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, and I'd double the effort on the newsletter, because it gives me something to show. I'd try for startups and small firms where the finance person does lots of things. I'd also take any freelance dashboard job that came up, even at a low rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. I'm optimistic by nature, but this much waiting wears down the optimism. Greta tells me to give it time, and I try to hold on to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are you using AI in your own search right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interview prep: I give it the job ad and ask for ten likely questions, then I answer out loud and ask for feedback. I also use it to tidy my spreadsheets. I never send a letter without rewriting it, because the first draft always sounds like a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the newsletter do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newsletter gives me a small audience and a habit of explaining things clearly. A recruiter at a small firm told me she'd read it, which was a thrill. The newsletter doesn't pay yet, but it's the only thing in my week that's growing.

say: I'd say it's a **decent tool**, like a calculator, and not a miracle.
I'd tell friends it's only great when you know what you're **asking**.
think: My situation wouldn't change: **no offer**, some debt and about two months saved.
do: Keep applying, focusing on **startups** and small firms where finance does many jobs.
Double the effort on my student **newsletter** to have something to show.
Take any **freelance dashboard** job, even at a low rate.
feel: **Uneasy**, with optimism worn thin by the waiting.
S0.quote: The newsletter doesn't pay yet, but it's the only thing in my week that's growing.
fieldNote: Freya is an **optimist under strain**: she keeps producing, but the no-offer limbo is wearing her down.
Her AI use is practical and disciplined; she rewrites anything she sends.
She is the only one of the nine with a public project, which gives her real evidence for recruiters.

steps.text: Apply to startups and small firms where finance does many jobs
Publish the student money newsletter every week
Take freelance dashboard work at a low rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the first time I've seen the ground shift under finance. Planning, checking and reporting will be done with tools, and the people who steer them get ahead. I'd tell friends to learn them now, because waiting helps no one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the entry-level pile gets smaller, and the people with real tool skills sit at the top of it. I'm good at tools, but so are others, so I'd need more. It's a race where the finish line keeps moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on the tools: build three dashboards for real small businesses and put them on a simple website. I'd learn the basics of data analysis properly, with a short course on SQL. I'd also pitch the startup where I interned, Pennant & Pine, to take me on a part-time contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but wired. It's a bit like being on a fast train that you're also trying to steer. There's adrenaline, but I'd rather there was a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your own advantage over other graduates come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've built something real with the tools, and most of my classmates have only tried them. But that gap closes within a year, so I can't rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine, but that her job is safe for longer than mine. Greta changes dressings and talks to scared families. I'd say money is the thing I'd want us to plan together, because two incomes in one flat is a strength.

say: I'd say this is the first time the ground has shifted under **finance**.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools **now**, because waiting helps no one.
think: The entry-level pile gets **smaller**, and people with real tool skills sit at the top.
My tool skill is an edge, but **others** will have it too.
do: Build **three dashboards** for real small businesses and put them on a website.
Take a **SQL course** to learn data analysis properly.
Pitch **Pennant & Pine** for a part-time contract.
feel: **Anxious but wired**, like steering a fast train and wishing for a driver.
S1.quote: I've built something real with the tools, and most of my classmates have only tried them.
fieldNote: Freya sees her edge as **temporary**, a clear and unsentimental read.
Her plan is portfolio-first: dashboards for real clients, pitched to a firm she knows.
Greta's nursing job offers contrast and shared-income comfort.

steps.text: Build three dashboards for real small businesses and post them online
Take a SQL course to learn data analysis properly
Pitch Pennant & Pine for a part-time contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about people, not just tools. Two years is far too short for schools or firms, so the government needs to catch the fall. I'd share every useful resource I find with other graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think most junior finance jobs go within the first year of that. My skills are the right ones for the wrong time: I'm good with tools, but the tools are replacing the job I'd use them in. Even being the best isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my overheads tiny by staying in the room with Greta and cooking everything. I'd go all in on building a one-person service, like finance dashboards and reports for small firms, priced low. And I'd talk to everyone about how they're coping, because I'd want to see which shapes of work survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can feel it in my stomach when I picture it. But I'm also the kind who'd want to start moving that same night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, the day after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Open my spreadsheet and list every skill I have and what each one could be sold for to a person, not a company. Then message ten small business owners I know and ask what's hurting them. That's the first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your adaptability stop helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When there are no jobs to adapt into. Learning fast gets you into rooms, but if the rooms are closing, the speed doesn't matter. At that point it's about whether the system helps, which I can't control.

say: I'd say we need to talk about **people**, not just tools.
I'd say the government must **catch the fall**, because two years is too short for schools and firms.
think: Most junior finance jobs go **within a year**, and I'm good at the tools replacing them.
Even being the **best** isn't a plan.
do: Keep **costs tiny** by staying in my sister's room and cooking everything.
Launch a **one-person service** making dashboards and reports for small firms.
Ask ten **small business owners** what is hurting them.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a knot in my stomach, but ready to move that night.
S2.quote: Learning fast gets you into rooms, but if the rooms are closing, the speed doesn't matter.
fieldNote: Freya's adaptability is real but she knows its **limits**: it can't create jobs.
First-week plan is specific: skills list, ten calls to business owners.
Anger is directed at the system, not at herself.

steps.text: Stay in my sister's room and cook everything to keep rent low
Launch a low-priced dashboard and reporting service for small firms
Call ten small business owners to learn what hurts them
Join a local campaign for graduate income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real window: long enough to prepare, short enough to be urgent. I'd tell people to start side projects now and stop waiting for permission. And I'd say employers should train juniors, since they'll need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but in control. I'd get a first job where I can use the tools, build a track record, and make myself the person who runs the finance engine for a small company. That's a job that's hard to replace entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a role at a smaller firm, because you get more responsibility sooner. I'd keep the newsletter and turn it into something paid, like a short course for students. And I'd invest a bit each month in an index fund, because I expect my income to bump around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but fine, like before a big presentation. I know it's coming, and I'd rather be preparing than pretending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for how you plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd have time to try three things and keep the one that works. In two years I'd get one attempt. With ten I might get complacent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skills would you bet on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bet on explaining numbers to people, judging risk and running a small business end to end. Those require trust and judgement as well as speed, and I enjoy them.

say: I'd say five years is a **real window**, long enough to prepare and short enough to be urgent.
I'd tell people to start **side projects** now and stop waiting for permission.
think: I'd feel **anxious but in control**, building a track record in a first job.
Running finance for a small company is hard to **replace entirely**.
do: Take a role at a **smaller firm** for more responsibility sooner.
Turn my newsletter into a **paid short course** for students.
Invest a bit monthly in an **index fund**, expecting uneven income.
feel: **Anxious but fine**, like before a big presentation.
S3.quote: With five years I'd have time to try three things and keep the one that works.
fieldNote: Five years suits Freya's **try-and-keep** style; she wants room for experiments.
She bets on trust-heavy skills: explaining numbers, judging risk, running a small company.
Mixed income idea, wages plus course plus index fund, is consistent with her adaptability.

steps.text: Take a finance role at a smaller firm with more responsibility
Turn the newsletter into a paid short course for students
Invest a fixed amount monthly in an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to build something good, like retraining that's actually useful and a fairer way to share the gains. I'd tell friends this is the time to explore without panic. And I'd say it's not an excuse to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. I could build a career, maybe a small company, maybe travel. I'd still keep learning, because I'd rather be early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, grow the newsletter into a proper small business and learn one new skill a year. I'd save for a deposit and eventually get my own place, so Greta and I aren't sharing a bedroom at thirty. I'd also volunteer teaching money basics in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and a bit excited. It's the first picture where I imagine a life in detail: where I'd live, what I'd do on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you can't do with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could start a business, change careers once, and still have time for a second attempt. Ten years is enough to fail at something and recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and miss the moment things speed up. I'd set a reminder every year to check what's changed and update my skills.

say: I'd say we have time to build **something good**, like useful retraining and a fairer share of gains.
I'd say this is no excuse to **wait**.
think: I'd be **calm**, with time for a career, maybe a small company, maybe travel.
I'd keep learning, since I'd rather be **early than late**.
do: Get a first job and grow the newsletter into a **small business**.
Learn **one new skill** a year and save for a deposit.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, able to picture a Saturday in that life.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to fail at something and recover.
fieldNote: Freya is the most **relaxed** here: ten years gives her room to fail and recover.
She plans a yearly check-in so comfort doesn't make her miss the speed-up.
Wanting her own place shows what's at stake in her private life.

steps.text: Take a first job and grow the newsletter into a small business
Learn one new skill every year
Save for a deposit on my own place
Teach money basics in local schools as a volunteer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I love a plan and that one doesn't give me time to make one. I'm fine with change, but even I need more than two years to turn my life around. What would help is practical: a way to earn while I retrain, honest information from employers, and the freedom to try things without losing my safety net.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that adaptable people get told they'll be fine, and that's not quite true. I can learn fast, but if there are no jobs, learning fast doesn't create any. I'd like to see the people in charge worry about the jobs, not just the tools.

headlineQuote: Adaptable people get told they'll be fine, and that's not quite true.
portrait: **Freya** is a 23-year-old graduate in business and finance, top of her class, sharing a bedroom with her sister Greta, a nurse.
She is **pragmatic**, uses AI daily, and runs a small student money newsletter.
Her internships at a startup and an insurer showed her the **tools-first** side of finance.
She moves early in every scenario, building skills and **side projects**, while saying adaptability can't create jobs.
Her mood runs from uneasy to alarmed in the 2-year world and settles to calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, because even an adaptable person needs more than two years to turn her life around.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and a way to earn while she learns.
Honest **information from employers** about hiring, and a safety net so she can try things without risking everything.
